title: A blessed night
hookLine: We sent it down on a blessed night (44:3)
carry: a night better than a thousand months

lines: A BOOK THAT NAMES ITS NIGHT.
cards: Plenty of books never say when they were written. The Qur'an speaks of its own coming down more than once, and here it names not a year or a season but a night.

Surah Ad-Dukhan, the Smoke, the forty-fourth surah, begins with two Arabic letters, Ha and Mim, whose meaning, scholars say, Allah knows best. Then an oath by the book itself, and then, in the third verse, a time stamp.
Not a date. A quality. The night it came down was blessed.

teach.h: HA. MIM. AN OATH BY THE BOOK.
teach.b: Pickthall's translation of the opening: "Ha. Mim. By the Scripture that maketh plain. Lo! We revealed it on a blessed night." The Arabic for blessed night is laylatin mubarakah.
Mubarak comes from baraka, a word you may know from a greeting card: Eid Mubarak.

teach.h: MUBARAK: BLESSING THAT STAYS AND GROWS.
teach.b: Baraka is blessing that stays and grows, the way a little food somehow feeds a whole table. So which night is it?

teach.h: MOST SAY: THE NIGHT OF POWER.
teach.b: Ibn Kathir and most commentators say it's the night named in Surah Al-Qadr, the ninety-seventh surah: Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, which hadith place in the last ten nights of Ramadan.
Surah Al-Baqarah also says the Qur'an was revealed in the month of Ramadan, and putting those verses together, that reading became the common one.
A minority of early voices connected this verse to the middle night of Sha'ban instead, and some Muslims still keep that night with prayer, but Ibn Kathir and others held to Ramadan.

The next verse says that on this night every wise matter is made distinct, and commentators read that as the affairs of the coming year being set out, part of why people spend that night in prayer. And why a night at all?
The Qur'an keeps coming back to the dark hours: rising for prayer while others sleep, the night as a covering.

teach.h: A NIGHT, WHEN THE NOISE STOPS.
teach.b: A night is when the noise stops. The sources don't explain why this book arrived after sunset rather than at noon, and it's honest to say so.
But the people who keep the Night of Power answer with their feet: they stay awake, they pray, they read, waiting for a night better than a thousand months.

how: Many Muslims spend the odd nights of the last ten days of Ramadan in extra prayer and Qur'an reading, seeking Laylat al-Qadr; some also keep the middle night of Sha'ban, and many pray a short night prayer before dawn year round.

practice: Let the room go quiet, and picture the last real dark you remember: a sleeping house, one lamp, nobody needing you. Breathe there for a minute. If you pray, say alhamdulillah slowly into that quiet; if you don't, just rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Baraka, blessing that stays and grows, the root behind the blessed night Ad-Dukhan says the Qur'an came down on. Today's word.
